links.reason: 18 says the lute from Indra, got by the sage's grace, is one before which elephants and birds fall at the feet (கரிணமும் புள்ளும் கண்டடி வீழும் கீதப் ... யாழ்); 19 shows the elephant hearing the lute, bowing and offering its trunk (பணிந்தடி இறைஞ்சி நின்று). The later verse fulfils the power the earlier names; the allies-winning clause is outside the pair.

2057 asks Kama for union with Civakan's chest (காளை சீவகன் அகலம் சேர்த்தின்), and 908 does make Civakan an exception (சீவகன் ... பொருந்திற் பொருந்துக). But 908 has no word for chest or gold, and பொன்றும் சாகம் is unclear, so the 'exception was a waiting' reading and the disguised-song cause are read in.
links.text_issue: 908 line 2 பொன்றுஞ் சாகம் unclear; 'gold chest' not in the Tamil; 2057 repaired

links.reason: 256 has the prince see her playing ball (பந்தை ஆட ... குமரன் கண்டான்); 257 repeats the sight and has them unite in the grove (மயக்கமுற்று ... புணர்ந்தான்). That is story order; the teaches leans on her loss in 258, which the pair does not contain.

160 likens the king to Dharma, Varuna, Death, Vaman and the five-arrowed son of Tiru (அழகின் கணை ஐந்து உடைத் திருமகன்); Purananuru 56 likens the Pandya to four gods by wrath, strength, fame and purpose (கூற்றுஒத் தீயே, வலிஒத் தீயே). Both match a king to gods quality by quality, but inheritance is not shown, the 'flaw' and 'ironic edge' lie outside the verse, and வாமனே is unclear.

604 says their growing merit joined this pair (பொங்கு புண்ணியம் புணர்த்த ஆறு); Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out its own doer like a calf its mother (பழவினையும் அன்ன தகைத்து). The merit explaining the match is a loose fit with the deed that finds its doer, and the claim that the quatrain's cases usually fall on the wicked is not in the pair.

31 keeps both halves of the couplet (உயிர்நோய்செய் யாமை, உறுநோய் மறத்தல் against உற்றநோய் நோன்றல், உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை), adds not wronging others and giving up desire and anger, and ends that penance is not lowly but sweet (இழிவன்று இனிது தவம்). The change from bearing to forgetting pain and the answer to a doubt about lowliness are real extensions.

37 says Death does not yield to weeping or worship, so one should do penance; 39 says dying is easy and fullness of character hard (சாவது எளிது அரிது சான்றாண்மை). One is about Death's refusal, the other about ease against lasting virtue, so no incompatible claim about the same thing; the two share only the word death.

566 has the king bid the envoy show faultless virtues in sifted words (கோதிலாக் குணங்கள் தேற்றிக் கொழித்துரை); Kural 685 asks for brief, inoffensive, pleasing speech (தொகச் சொல்லி தூவாத நீக்கி). Both are about the envoy's speech, but brevity is not in 566, so the 'named standard' is not shown, and the 'host puts the envoy on trial' is a reading of one line.

206 bars putting wealth in the hands of untested eminent men or kin (சிறந்தார் தமரென்று தேற்றார்கை வையார்); 208 compares giving it to worthless men to rice kept by a crow (காக்கையைக் காப்பிட்ட சோறு). They give the same warning of two cases in separate verses of one chapter, so neither develops the other.

1752 has Civakan say death is better than living freed by a woman (பெண்இடர் விடுப்ப வாழ்வின் சாதலே நன்று); 1149 has Gandharvadattai say that a man freed by his wife loses his strength and learning's worth (ஆற்றலும் கல்வியும் என்). Both state the same honour code, but 'held by each without the other's knowing' is not shown and the marker ties 1752 to an earlier refusal of her spells.

1907 says that those who say trees have no life are madmen or ghouls (மரமுயிர் இல்லை என்பார் பித்தலர்); Neelakesi 370 has Mokkalan call the claim that trees have life a fault like madness (பித்தெழுந்தாரொப்ப). The two assert opposite things about plant life and each hurls madness at the other side, so the quarrel is live; the Cintamani verse names no school but its claim is the one Neelakesi defends.

1768 has her seal the letter with her flower earring (பூங்குழையாற் பொறி ஒற்றுபு) and send the companions; 1872 has the seal removed and the letter read (பொறியைப் புறநீக்குபு). That is the letter's delivery, already plot, and the seal 'guarding her words' is added by the note; the marker admits the earring in 1872 may be Civakan's own.

1592 explains the red as lac stains of women's feet laid to cure the tree's longing (அலத்தகச் சுவடு); 1593 has the jester turn it on the king, who blooms when the queen's foot touches his head (தேவியார் சீறடி சென்னி சேர்த்தலும் ... அலர்ந்திடு). The later verse applies the lesson as a jibe, which the first does not carry.

297 has the usurper take Fortune and have the drum beaten in his own name (தன் பெயரினால் பறை அறைந்தான்); 609 has drummers bless the lord who embraces the earth as his bride and the city. The verses do not say 609's lord is the usurper or that its drum is the same, and nothing in them is incompatible, so the teaching is read in.

63 traces suffering through births to harming living beings (மன்னுயிர்க் கொலையினால்); 36 says births would not follow if bodies had been given up and dharma practised (துறந்தறம் புணரின்). 36 already gives a cause, the lack of renunciation and dharma, so it does not 'only lament'; 63 names a different cause, which makes the pair a complement, not a development.

94 has the ministers say the elephant cannot pass the vina (கைவீணை கடவாது); 97 shows it hearing the lute and bowing at his feet (கேட்டு வந்தடி பணிந்தது). The later verse is the test of the earlier claim.

1235 puts hell for the meat-eater against a god's birth for the abstainer and has the hunter choose (ஊன்றினாது ஒழிந்து புத்தேளாவதே உறுதி); Kural 255 says that if one eats flesh hell will not open its mouth (அண்ணாத்தல் செய்யாது அளறு). The conversion by question gives the rule an answer, but 1235 has no image of a mouth that stays shut, so the epic does not gain it, and only the shared theme of meat is shown.

2245 likens Madanan to the moon swallowed by Rahu and plunging into the sea (கோளரா விழுங்க முந்நீர்க் குளித்ததே போல்); 2251 likens the Kalinga king to the sun falling into the sea with a planet (பருதி முந்நீர்க் கோளொடும் வீழ்வது). The celestial-fall image is shared in one battle, but that the two are 'both lights of one host' is not in the verses.

387 names the birth star Uttirattathi (உத்திரட்டாதி) and 404 says his horoscope made his words and beauty (சாதகம் செய்த). The star leading to the horoscope is plausible, but 404 does not name the star, and 'worth fixed before parentage was known' is not in either verse.

1005 has Civakan say the girdle, ornaments and anklets did penance to be worn by her (நோற்றன); 1017 says to Gandharvadattai that a swan of the Ganges would not go to the sand of a well. 1017 does not name the girl, so that it belittles the same woman is the marker's reading, and compliments fitted to two hearers are not incompatible claims.

244 says the king valued a woman's pleasure above heaven and nectar and the world sank with him (பெண்ணின் இன்பம் பெரிது எனத் தாழ்ந்து); Kural 906 says those who fear their wives' shoulders have no worth though they live like gods (அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சுபவர்). The epic's fault is indulgence, not fear of a wife, so 'the same comparison in reverse' is loose; the added public cost is real, but the epic does not apply the couplet.

1029 has lotuses close like chaste women when the beloved leaves (கற்புடை மகளிர் போல); Akananuru 71 has bees leave pool flowers like graceless men (நயன்இல் மாக்கள் போல). Both set an evening flower scene beside parting, but the figures differ (lotus and lily against bees), so a shared evening scene giving different blame is not shown.

1738 says the child grows guarded by women (மங்கையர் காப்ப வளர்கின்றான்); Naladiyar 20 warns that Death takes even the newborn while the mother wails. Nothing in 1738 speaks of death or its stealth, so reading the guarded growth against the quatrain is imposed by the note.

2355 has Civakan sleep through the cries of wounded and weeping women (இறைவன் கேளாத் துயிலேற்றான்); Mullaippattu 67-79 has the king sleepless, thinking of the wounded elephant, fallen men and horses (கண்படை பெறாஅது). The two kings' nights are a real contrast, but no claim conflicts, and 'peace of a finished war' against 'a war still going on' is read in.

1345 has the king shoot the arrow named Naama (நாம வாளி) and 1346 has the arrow cut the bow, shafts and illusion. That is the shot and its effect in order, already in the plot; 'outlasted every earlier shot' is not in the pair.

687 has Anangamalai cry ceaselessly to Civakan (அரற்றுமால்); 2593 has Civakan say 'how could I forget you' (மறப்பேனோ யான் நின்னை) and her joy. The later verse answers the cry, but its speaker and division are unclear and 'after the usurper's fall and a letter' is not in the pair.

67 has the king put aside the sword at the youth's own words and bow (மன்னவன் தன்கை வாளும் ... மாற்றி); 273 has him lay down anger and weapon at the merchant's gentle words (வணிகன் சொல் இகழாதே ... படையும் மாற்றி) but still scorn the dust-grimed man. The same gesture occurs for different causes, one ending in reverence and one leaving contempt.

7 praises Saccandan's கோடாத செங்கோல் and வாடாத வென்றி; 9 says desire grown dense made him deaf to counsel (காமம் கனைந்து சொல்லாறு கேளான்) and he was beaten by a plot. The scene refutes the praise, and the fall is put to the king's own desire, not to a stronger foe.

1916 has the ministers beg the sage to turn aside the tangled births (பிணங்கும் பிறவிகள் பேர்த்துய்மின்); 1920 has him list the states of rebirth, the deeds that fix them, the ways of conquering deeds and release (கதியும் ... வீட்டது மாண்பும்). The reply sets out what the answer will cover, beginning with the map of births, which the plea does not contain.

4 speaks of the opposing deed shed in order (மாறுறு கருமம் வரிசையின் உதிர்ப்பை), and the poet's last lines are hard to parse; Kural 380 says nothing is stronger than fate (ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள). Shedding deeds by ripening need not oppose fate, so the claimed 'room for undoing' rests on an uncertain reading.
links.text_issue: 4 flagged uncertain; lines 3-4 hard to parse

links.reason: 1426 has Asvagriva bid the spell take every human with none left (ஒருவர் இன்றிச் செகுத்திடு); Tirumanthiram 238 says an unlearned king who says 'kill' is worse than Death, who spares the good (கொல்லென்பான் ... காலன் நணுகநில்லான்). The Tirumanthiram fits the order as a judgment, but the epic's own verdict is not tested or changed by it, so the pair is an illustration.

1028 has birds settle with their young and mates while evening comes like a spear to the lover (மனத்துக் கெஃகாய் மாலை); Natrinai 69 has birds go to their young and an evening without pity for the wife (அருள் இல் மாலை). The happy birds against the sufferer are shared and meaningful, but Natrinai 69 lists a wide scene (stag, doe, jasmine, cows' bells), so the claim that it lacks the epic's wide view is false.

314 has ஊழிக் காலம் ஓடின said of Achuvakandan and 333 says the words said of him match ஊழியார் உரை. The echo of ஊழி is real, but both are flagged uncertain and the meaning of ஊழி (aeon, fate or elders) is not settled, so 'a doom the epic has already spoken' is read in.

1956 grades animal births from one sense to five (ஓரறிவாதி ... ஐம்பொறி ஈறா); Neelakesi 77 splits them into those that stand and those that move, the standing being of five kinds (நிற்பனவும் செல்பவும்). Both are Jain lists of animal life, but the verses do not themselves say how the two cuts fit, so 'two cuts of one classification' needs doctrine outside the Tamil.

2992 has the wives take off ornaments like a vine shedding flowers (பாசிழை நீக்குகின்றார்); Siddhar 19 asks when the singer will leave silk and gold and desire the feet. Only the ornaments are shared; neither qualifies the other, and the claim that the epic scene gets a god's feet as aim ignores that its renunciation is Jain.

535 has the first lord set up five royal lineages and make known their conduct and occupations (ஒழுக்கமுந் தொழிலுந் தோற்றி); Kural 133 says conduct is what makes noble birth (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை). The verse ties conduct to lineage by ordinance, not by earning, so the gains-claim that standing rests on conduct is not in it, and the verse is flagged uncertain.

267 calls the king god-like because he orders a man's lot in both worlds (இருமையும் ... இறைவன் போல); Kural 388 makes the just, protecting king இறை for the people. The shared word is இறை/இறைவன், but the verse's construction is unclear (marker flagged) and 'reaches the next world's lot' is one reading, so it is not a reason for the Kural's word.

52 says one whose anger never cools is to be avoided, for it is hard to trust one who never clears (தெளியானைத் தேறல் அரிது); Kural 510 warns against trusting the unexamined (தேரான் தெளிவு). The proverb applies the couplet's rule by naming a mark that fails the examination, with the wordplay on தெளி/தேறு holding both.

670 has the king reason from earlier deeds and from earlier kings who pleased the overlord (வேந்தர் ஒன்றி உவப்பித்து ஆண்ட); 685 has Tivittan say they would pay tribute only if shoulder and sword were of no use (தோளினும் ... வாளினும் பயன் எனை). The two answers to the same demand are incompatible, and the speakers are different, so it is a real tension on what a king owes.

248 has Dharmadattan say a king's splendour guards the earth even while he sleeps (உறங்கும் ஆயினும் மன்னவன் தன் ஒளி ... காக்கும்); 261 shows the king sunk in love, the army given up (தானை நீத்த வேந்தனை), with the minister planning his death. The scene refutes the claim in the same chapter.

2876 says the old deed clings through every body and burns the soul (தீவினை தொடர்ந்து நீங்கா); Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas end when the sunstone meets the sun, not before. 2876 names no remedy and mala is not simply karma, so 'the Saiva verse limits the Jain one's permanence' is the note's synthesis, and the epic-side gains-clause is not in either text.

264 says if kings give up the old way of guarding and the white parasols grow hot, ponds and groves are scorched (வெண்குடை வெதும்புமாயின்); Kural 389 puts the world under the parasol of a king who bears bitter words. The cool-shade image reversed is a real contrast, but 264's cause is giving up guarding, not losing patience, so the first gains-clause misstates the epic.

319 lists the Charana ascetics by their powers of travelling over flowers and waves (சாரணர்); 1177 says the Charanas at Aranapatham wash away their own karma (தம்வினை கழுவுகின்றார்). The shared class name is real, but there is no shared image, and joining a catalogue entry with a scene gives only a fact about the class, not a teaching.
